#### What this PR does / why we need it:


This PR reduces the amount of LB re-configurations for ETP=local services by removing the sync completely for any node readiness changes, from the CCM's sync loop. The referenced issue explains the problem in greater detail, so readers are henced directed to that for what concerns the genesis of the problem. A lot has been discussed in this PR and a plan forward has been drafted. The following summarizes the discussion:

- Remove syncs w.r.t node state changes in the CCM in 1.25 (follow up PR, once this merges, is to be expected for remaining node conditions) 
- Maybe / possibly / hopefully backport that to the oldest supported Kube version also supporting ETP=local services
- Have the reported status of the LB HC configured for ETP=local services reflect the node state in 1.25 (also in the form of a follow up PR)
- Write KEP for dealing with transitioning node state for all service LBs. 
-  Kube >= after KEP : remove the sync logic for node state changes for all services and move them to the HC 


#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:

Partially fixes #111539 for ETP=local services, specifically: reduces the amount of cloud API calls and service downtime caused by excessive re-configurations of all cluster LBs as an effect of transitioning node readiness state.

```release-note
Reduce the number of cloud API calls and service downtime caused by excessive re-configurations of cluster LBs with externalTrafficPolicy=Local when node readiness changes (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/111539). The service controller (in cloud-controller-manager) will avoid resyncing nodes which are transitioning between `Ready` / `NotReady` (only for for ETP=Local Services). The LBs used for these services will solely rely on the health check probe defined by the `healthCheckNodePort` to determine if a particular node is to be used for traffic load balancing. 
```

/assign @bowei -- I'm very interested in poking more at the lifecycle of the LB node

Some additional notes here below from the recent discussion in sig-net that just ended. Also, you'll be able to find the slides presented by me, here: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1EsK5FLS4s6E3Ok42XhRz643YtB9uZHn3wohWvcMyHag/edit#slide=id.p

My third slide present some ideas around the possibility of removing everything the CCM does w.r.t synchronizing nodes transitioning between `NotReady` <-> `Ready`.  

1. Is this PR - which eliminates the mentioned sync for ETP=local services, from the CCM's node sync loop
2. Is removing that sync completely for all services irrespective of ETP=local or not. 
a. Is removing that sync completely _only_ for a selected set of services, indicated by the user through the utilization of an annotation on the service object 
3. Is removing that sync completely for ETP=local services from the CCM, but replacing it by having kube-proxy dial the kubelet's read-only port when answering to the probe executed by the LB against the `HealthCheckNodePort`. I.e: kube-proxy would keep the current behavior (validating that the node in question is actually hosting endpoints for the service) and AND-ing that with the kubelet's reported state. That means that the LB would continue executing one probe against the `HealthCheckNodePort`, but kube-proxy would open a local connection against kubelet's read-only port on the node for every LB probe. There was some confusion surrounding this during the meeting, hence why I've chosen to detail this here. This would result in the same behavior as today, but be much more dynamic and efficient at handling transitioning node state - where instead of re-configuring the LB with a new set of nodes, the LB simply probes the node on the `HealthCheckNodePort` as it currently does, with the result also reflecting the kubelet/node readiness state. 
4. Is removing that sync completely for _all_ services from the CCM. Instead we define a standardised behavior for health checking nodes which are listed as backends for `LoadBalancer` type services, that all cloud provider implementations must adhere to. All cloud providers today implement this interface: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/cloud-provider/cloud.go#L133-L162 , however: when the service is ETP != local they are free to specify custom probes on their LBs. What they do today was described at the bottom of the description to this PR. If we align the behavior for all cloud implementations: we could have them include a probe against the kubelet's read-only port - or do as in the ETP=local case and have the LB query kube-proxy which does multiple checks. In the end, LB's only really care to know if the node can service traffic and if the service `NodePort` on the node is reachable. All three clouds have chosen one of these two checks, not both. GCE's LB check is actually superfluous, since the CCM also checks the same condition (i.e: the kubelet state/node readiness).  

3 and 4. will require enhancement proposal and are beyond the scope of this PR, but we can discuss them here (or I can open a KEP for them and we can discuss them there...?)

This PR only concerns itself with finding a solution to either 1. and/or 2., simply because this currently is a bug for clusters at scale and, I believe, we should backport the fix to older releases. 

I am actually in favour of doing 2.a., meaning: modifying this PR slightly and removing any relation to ETP=local services and checking where endpoints are hosted. I would instead prefer we define an annotation (ex: `service.beta.kubernetes.io/lb-ignore-node-not-ready`) which a user can set on the service object to tell the CCM to ignore this service for node readiness changes. The implementation effort would be minimal and would allow the user to solve both problems presented in my first slides. I, as a user of Kubernetes, should be allowed to disable the CCM's sync for node readiness state if I don't want my LBs to be re-configured as a cause by that. I own my nodes and LBs and should thus be allowed to decide what's best.

If we can't agree on 2.a, then 1. (the current state of this PR) will at least help reduce the time taken to sync all LBs by the CCM on large clusters with a lot of services ETP=local, which is already an improvement from today.

Thinking more about this: For node-centric LB setups, there are 3 states a Node can be in wrt LB backend sets:

1) The node is not in the LB set(s)
2) The node is in the LB set(s) but the LB's healthcheck to that node is failing
3) The node is in the LB set(s) and the LB's healthcheck to that node is passing

Today we consider a variety of distinct signals. which add up to mild chaos:
* Is the Node Ready (as per Conditions)?
* Is the LB's healthcheck to that node passing?
* Does the node have the "exclude" label?
* Does the node have to-be-deleted taint?
* Is the node Unschedulable?

With the caveat that different implementations have different healthcheck capabilities, I think that we should decide and document the ideal mapping of these individual inputs to the 3 primary states, with an emphasis on minimizing API calls to the management plane while delivering the most-correct behavior possible (and to be clear I think we are NOT most-correct today).

I posit that the ONLY reasons to move a node out of the LB set are "administrative action" - specifically someone set the `node.kubernetes.io/exclude-from-external-load-balancers` label.  Otherwise, once it is in the LB set, we should leave it there and rely on healthchecks.

Why?  Two reasons.

1) As evidenced by this PR, adding/removing from the set is expensive and should be avoided when possible.
2) In some clouds there is a distinction between "in the LB set but failing HC" and "not in the LB set".   In the case of the former, existing flows are preserved but new connections will avoid the node.  In the case of the latter, existing flows are broken.  Keeping the LB in the set means we can at least TRY to service existing connections.

![Node_LB_states](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/5595220/178065317-3629ecb6-4816-49c2-8b21-74c06b062661.png)

How?  The healthchecks we set up for LBs need to be smarter.  We can build this into kube-proxy (and every other kube-proxy equivalent) or we can build a different mechanism - TBD.

This is obviously not helpful RIGHT NOW to this PR, but directionally - thoughts?
@swetharepakula -- (see above diagram) -- this likely intersects with the endpoints lifecycle work

> This is obviously not helpful RIGHT NOW to this PR, but directionally - thoughts?

I completely agree. And is also why I gravitated towards an enhancement proposal for this with an initial first draft of said proposal being: modifying the health check probes to what I mentioned in point [3. and 4. here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/109706#issuecomment-1112737473) . This should address the issue of reacting more efficiently to node state changes without also needing to re-configuring the LB on the cloud provider's side and disrupting ingress/egress traffic. 

I can start writing up the proposal, if we agree that we need it.   

I also want to emphasize that the referenced issue just above (#102367) will not get fixed by this PR if they don't have a large amount of ETP=local services, only mentioning this https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/102367#issuecomment-1179400517 mentions "I think the 'real fix' is related", and I want to set the expectation to anyone reading that, that: it is if you have a lot of "ETP=local" services, otherwise this won't fix anything.

Updated the PR, taking into account the code review thus far.

> I can start writing up the proposal, if we agree that we need it.

Yeah, I think your #4 is close to what I have in mind, though I don't think it's necessarily kubelet's healthz that LBs should probe - this is a place to explore options and tradeoffs.

Worth a KEP, I think.

> Something smells wrong, but it took me a moment to fput my finger on it...

You are right, I overlooked that case. We need to track the last successfully configured set of nodes, per service, and if a node transitions from Ready -> NotReady we'll need to sync if the node wasn't in the last configured set. That should take care of the case you mentioned: 

Nodes A, B, C are ready.
Service S with ETP=local running on nodes A, B.
LB set for S is {A, B, C}.
Node A goes Unready.
We remove A from the LB set, now {B, C}.
Pod on A is removed.
Node A goes Ready.
We don't ignore it even if it has no endpoints, because A is not in the last configured set {B,C}.
Start a new S pod on node A.

vs 

Nodes A, B, C are ready.
Service S with ETP=local running on nodes A, B.
LB set for S is {A, B, C}.
Node C goes Unready.
We ignore it because no endpoints.
Node C goes Ready.
We ignore it because no endpoints.
Start a new S pod on node C.

Doing this complicates matters a bit, because keeping track of the set of configured nodes per service required a bit of change to have the tests pass in `-race` mode, while at the same time not serializing the initiated parallelization over `nodeSyncService`...

...moreover, if we still want to be paranoid about spurious resyncs of nodes we also need to keep track of "last global set of synced nodes". That causes one test case to result in a "sub-optimal" solution 🤷  

I split that part out into its own commit so that we can decide on a better implementation or if we are to keep it or not. 

Also, I've extended the tests with more cases...this made the PR go XL I think. 

> Worth a KEP, I think. 

I will get to drafting that then.

So this is now pretty complex.  I assert that we don't REALLY want any of this - we really want something like the diagram above, which should totally solve the problem and not need any of this complexity (so this ends up being reverted).

I'm also worried about possible other implementations, like GCP's ILB subsetting, not being kept in sync.

What if we, instead, actually tackled the real issue?  I strarted this a while back, though I feel like this could use some cleanup:  https://github.com/thockin/kubernetes/commit/9dd360185becfb972c7777f7c83b5246909c3df9

Specifically, what if we :

1) Change service controller to NOT EXCLUDE unready, unschedulable, and tained nodes.  LBs would be given all nodes that are not excluded by the specific exclsuion label.

2) Change kube-proxy to watch its own Node and make healthz fail if the node is Unready, Unschedulable, or ToBeDeleted tainted.

Results: 

* LB impls that use that healthz will work better.
 
* LB impls that don't use that healthz will see nodes that they didn't see before.  I argue that this may be acceptable because:
  - if the node is legit dead, the LB needs some HC anyway which will cover this
  - if the node is being drained (unschedulable) or being deleted (tainted) then the eventual node removal is just as abrupt as removing it from the LB set (no opportunity to drain), so "not worse than before".

* In the face of version skew (older kube-proxy, newer control-plane), LB impls will see nodes that they didn't see before.   See previous point.

* We could make a new URL (e.g. /readyz) but then we need to wait until the oldest supported kube-proxy supports this, which means introducing the kube-proxy change, waiting a year, then implementing the controller half.  I don't think that is warranted, given the above.

* We need to update alternative implementations (e.g. Cilium, Antrea(?), etc) to also HC-fail in these node situations.

It's a deeper change but it's actually one we want to keep.  What do you all think?  Am I trivializing the risks?

> So this is now pretty complex 

Yes, I agree...but you should see the work-arounds to this problem that users are thinking about deploying.

 > I assert that we don't REALLY want any of this - we really want something like the diagram above, which should totally solve the problem and not need any of this complexity (so this ends up being reverted).

I 100 % agree that we want that diagram. The reason as to why I never started doing that was because I supposed that an enhancement proposal would be required for such a change. Wouldn't doing such a thing diverge the implementation / expectation that is already set by different Kubernetes service proxies? I thought that's the point of the enhancement proposal and why we do them to begin with: to align and coordinate different implementations/vendors, so that users don't suffer.

If that is not the case I could obviously modify this PR (or build on your: https://github.com/thockin/kubernetes/commit/9dd360185becfb972c7777f7c83b5246909c3df9) to implement that mechanism instead. 

One thing though, in your diagram you noted: 

> It's really about whether the on-node proxy mechanism is up-to-date and ready to handle traffic 

but isn't that already the case for ETP=local services through the usage of `healthCheckNodePort` probe? That probe from the LB to the proxy evaluates precisely if the proxy on each node can respond, and moreover: even execute logic which determines if the service has an endpoint on the node. If we want to implement that diagram for ETP=local services, we might as well just remove the current CCM logic for ETP=local services altogether. Just configure LBs with the full set of nodes (minus the ones with the exclusion label) and avoid re-configuring LBs if nodes experience readiness changes.   

My hope and original goal _with this PR_ was to back-port this PR to older releases once we have something we agree upon...but given the turn this discussion is taking, maybe that was a wild dream. But in that case I would even say: let's not do anything for now and instead write up an enhancement proposal with a long term vision for this that includes all service proxies/CNI plugins and cloud providers. 

> Am I trivializing the risks? 

I can't speak for that fully since I lack visibility into the LB part on the cloud provider's side to tell, but I don't see why. The current problem (re-configuring all LBs for every node change in a cluster) in the CCM is a rather important issue. Implementing the mentioned behaviour would keep the functional behaviour aligned with the current, but be more efficient. It's more of having all stakeholders aligned on the expectations.

> The reason as to why I never started doing that was because I supposed that an enhancement proposal would be required for such a change

It would, but that doesn't mean "Oh no, it will take 18 months".  It just means we document the changes and tradeoffs BEFORE we make them in code.  It will require some outreach and "doing the legwork", of course but it's not fatal.  The main drawback is that the KEP window for 1.25 is already closed, so it could not  be launched until 1.26, really.

> I thought that's the point of the enhancement proposal and why we do them to begin with: to align and coordinate different implementations/vendors, so that users don't suffer.

I *think* we can do it in a way that is "not worse than today", which alleviates a lot of the pain.

> One thing though, in your diagram you noted:
>
>> It's really about whether the on-node proxy mechanism is up-to-date and ready to handle traffic
>
> but isn't that already the case for ETP=local services through the usage of healthCheckNodePort probe? That probe from the LB to the proxy evaluates precisely if the proxy on each node can respond, and moreover: even execute logic which determines if the service has an endpoint on the node. 

Sort of.  I took a quick peek at this and it seems to only check if there are any local endpoints.

We have one handler (pkg/proxy/healthcheck/proxier_health.go) which actually considers whether the proxy is healthy (though I am skeptical that it is really that robust, in looking at it again).

For ETP=Local we have another handler (pkg/proxy/healthcheck/service_health.go) which only considers whether therer are local endpoints.

That 2nd one should probably be the AND of both.

I'm saying that both of these should ALSO consider `unschedulable` and `ToBeDeleted` taints.  But even if they don't it's not a huge deal (I think - this is where we need some extra eyeballs).

> If we want to implement that diagram for ETP=local services, we might as well just remove the current CCM logic for ETP=local services altogether. Just configure LBs with the full set of nodes (minus the ones with the exclusion label) and avoid re-configuring LBs if nodes experience readiness changes.

Now THAT is a good idea.  I think we should *probably* do this for all Services, but doing it JUST for ETP=Local could be the first move.  That solves your problem without adding all the endpoints logic and moves us closer to where we want to be.

At the same time, we could change the endpoints to be more robust, and get that rolling out.  Since that is just moving equivalent logic from the service controller to the HC, I don't think we need a KEP.  The service logic remains in place, except ETP=Local.

The only real behavioral change, other than avoiding LB set syncs, is this:  In the face of version skew (an old kube-proxy with a new control-plane) an ETP=Local LB service will send traffic to nodes which are Unready or Unschedulable or tainted, but _only if_ those nodes have at least one endpoint for the Service.    And I still posit that this is OK - if the node goes hard-down, we have the same abrupt termination situation.  If the node is cleanly drained, those endpoints will go away.

1.25 could include the improved HCs and ETP=Local change.  During 1.26 we could KEP and discuss the equivalent for everyone else.

> My hope and original goal with this PR was to back-port this PR to older releases

If we just disable Unready-sync for ETP=Local, backporting is POSSIBLE, but we'll need to really justify it, That may be tough.

> The main drawback is that the KEP window for 1.25 is already closed, so it could not be launched until 1.26, really.

OK, I will need to focus on some other tasks for a couple of days, but I will get the enhancement proposal going ASAP, as to try to meet the 1.26 deadlines. 

> Now THAT is a good idea. I think we should probably do this for all Services, but doing it JUST for ETP=Local could be the first move. That solves your problem without adding all the endpoints logic and moves us closer to where we want to be.

Great! I will update this PR with that logic. My misunderstanding of what get placed in the "this change really needs a KEP before we can do anything" bucket was flawed, otherwise I would have done that from the get-go. 

> If we just disable Unready-sync for ETP=Local, backporting is POSSIBLE, but we'll need to really justify it, That may be tough.

Who do we need to justify it to? Maybe we can start poking people on this?

I think removing the CCM's LB set sync for ETP=local is an improvement from today, even without any change to any HC. Large clusters experience more entropy, entropy leads to more LB re-configuration, LB re-configuration leads to impacted SLAs. The changes leading to increased entropy might not have any relation to the service answering to that SLA...but currently it might/will.

I think this discussion really boils down to: "what does a node going NotReady really say about the networking state of the node?" - I feel like we don't know the answer. And maybe that should be the first question to work out on the enhancement proposal 

We had similar discussions/questions in OpenShift concerning what actions surrounding networking components should take for nodes that experience transient state to the negative - should we forward traffic to them or start ignoring them? I think we just based/copied the assumptions made by Kube...I was never sure that was correct, and I still am not. Like, in terms of causality: is there really any networking failure that will transition the node into `NotReady`, besides the classic and evident "CNI plugin hasn't written it's config file to disk". But that's more like a day 0 issue which means we probably don't have any endpoints on the node in any case, because nothing could be started. Then again, the kubelet going wonky might be because there's disk/CPU/memory pressure on the node, which might be impacting the kernel too, which might be impacting networking. But this is very speculative. I don't think there's ever been a clear and definitive networking test perform by the kubelet, which would place the node in the failed state and justify a load balancer/router/proxy/other node to stop sending traffic to the node in question - especially if the load balancer/router/proxy/other node already uses a dedicated probe to test if it can communicate with the pod/kube-proxy/node and _that passes_. So either we think of such a test that the kubelet could perform as to have NotReady actually mean that "this node should stop receiving traffic", or we agree that no such test can be designed because "networking is hard" and we just rely on HC and stop thinking about the node's readiness state for what concerns routing network traffic. 

I am saying this because even ETP=cluster services enable a health check from the LB to the nodes (on the major public cloud providers), as I mentioned in my PR description:

> GCE: probes [10256](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/cluster/ports/ports.go#L39)
> AWS: if ELB: probes the first NodePort defined on the service spec.
> Azure: probes all NodePort defined on the service spec. 

So maybe we should remove the CCMs LB set syncs, for all services without any change to any HC? That's maybe asking too much, or asking for trouble....

About backporting: would we want to backport the complicated current fix which keeps the behaviour almost aligned with current, i.e: disable unready-sync for nodes with no endpoints? Or just disable unready-sync altogether, knowing that we won't replace it in the HC? 

I am thinking:

Kube < 1.25 - complicated-but-fully-aligned-with-current-behavior-fix in the CCM for ETP=local
Kube = 1.25 - simple fix (disable unready+taint-sync) for ETP=local in the CCM and place them in the ETP=local HC
Kube >= 1.26 (or whenever the KEP gets in) - disable all checks in the CCM and place them in the HC corresponding to each service type

>> Now THAT is a good idea. I think we should probably do this for all Services, but doing it JUST for ETP=Local could be the first move. That solves your problem without adding all the endpoints logic and moves us closer to where we want to be.
>
> Great! I will update this PR with that logic. My misunderstanding of what get placed in the "this change really needs a KEP before we can do anything" bucket was flawed, otherwise I would have done that from the get-go.

I should be clear - I am playing a little fast-and-loose here, and we'll need to make a solid argument that this is actually OK.  I'm arguing that this is "reasonably safe" and "not worse than" before, but that CAN be argued.  Practically speaking, the PR as it stands is ALSO a risk - it's significantly more complex and could easily cause problems at scale for large clusters.  We've KEP'ed for less.  That really means that this probably CAN'T go into 1.25 as a "bug fix".

So I think we make the case for the simpler service controller change, limited to ETP=Local.  If we lose that case, we KEP and punt to 1.26.   Worst case we end up at 26 either way.

>> If we just disable Unready-sync for ETP=Local, backporting is POSSIBLE, but we'll need to really justify it, That may be tough.
>
> Who do we need to justify it to? Maybe we can start poking people on this?

Branch owners - their incentive is to keep branches stable.  This is not a zero-risk change, but again, I think we have a decent argument for "not worse".

> I think this discussion really boils down to: "what does a node going NotReady really say about the networking state of the node?" - I feel like we don't know the answer. And maybe that should be the first question to work out on the enhancement proposal

Agree.  It could mean the node has crashed.  It could mean the kubelet has crashed but network is OK.  It could mean the kubelet restarted and is figuring itself out.  It could mean the node is being drained, but is still serving in the meantime.  Are there other ways it could happen?  It has little actual correlation to whether that node can be used as an LB backend.

We should do a broader survey of LB implementations to see what they do for LB healthchecks.  I assume most of them do SOMETHING reasonable.  That means that, if the node legit crashed the HC would catch it.  If the kubelet crashed or restarted, who cares - we can (and should!) still serve traffic.  The really interesting case is when the node is being drained.  For ETP=Local services any pods will eventually be deleted, so continuing to serve traffic is correct.  So what about other service LBs, which just use the node as a "hop"?  Before this change, a draining node (unschedulable or tainted ToBeDeleted) is IMMEDIATELY removed from the LB set, abruptly terminating all connections. issue_context.title: [scale] node state changes causes excessive LB re-configurations
issue_context.body:
### What happened?

There is scale bug related to the cloud-controller-manager, namely: when a cluster reaches a state where the relation between the amount of LBs and cluster nodes reaches an almost equal amount (i.e: a many-to-many relation between LBs and nodes) the amount of cloud API calls performed by the CCM to sync LBs can become overwhelming for the cloud provider. This can (among other things) lead to:

1. an excessive amount of cloud API calls for the LB re-configurations
2. rate limiting by the cloud provider as an effect of 1.
3. or worse: a non-trivial amount of time to sync all services in the cluster, leading to desynchronized LBs.

An example of problem 3. is: imagine we have 200 LBs and 500 nodes, on clusters at such scale, the amount of events processed by the CCM for transitioning node state can become important. The current implementation of the CCM will resync all 200 LB services for any node which has a transitioning state - as to keep the LBs' configured backends in sync with the state of the cluster. It has been observed that on clusters at that scale, the cloud provider can take up to hours to process a full resync for all services. A scenario such as the below is hence not improbable (and actually quite likely):

1. Node25 transitions from Ready -> NotReady
[All LB services are synced - time taken for this might be long]
2. Service1's LB which only has an endpoint on Node25 gets Node25 removed from its list of backend
3. Node25 transitions from NotReady -> Ready again, cancelling the scheduled eviction for the endpoint hosted on Node25 for Service1
4. CCM is still processing the updated caused by 1. and clients connecting to the LB of Service1 continues experiencing connectivity issues, even though Node25 now is in a Ready state.
[Eventually - once the CCM enters its second reconciliation loop caused by 3.]
5. The LB for Service1 gets Node25 added to its list of backend again and connectivity is again achieved by clients.

The sync function which is triggered when a node transitions state from Ready <-> NotReady, is currently correct but can be avoided for services which have ExternalTrafficPolicyLocal if the service does not have an endpoint on any of the nodes which are transitioning state between Ready <-> NotReady. This is because such services are not designed to forward traffic to any other node, and the update is thus useless to them. The node which is experiencing a transitioning state is already configured for that LB, and the fact that it transitions state is a moot point for what concerns these services. 

The longer vision I have for this: remove the sync function for transitioning node readiness state from the CCM altogether and instead have all services of type LoadBalancer evaluate the node's readiness state by the utilization of a LB configured health check probe against the [kubelet's read-only port](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/cluster/ports/ports.go#L33). This would allow transitioning node readiness state to be handled much more dynamically (similar to what has already been implemented for HealthCheckNodePort by kube-proxy) for all services of type LoadBalancer irrespectively of if they define ExternalTrafficPolicyLocal or not....but that will require a enhancement proposal since cloud providers have divergent implementations of how they configure health check probes for LB services.

I am putting this here for completeness sake: this is what the major cloud providers currently do to health check services which are not ExternalTrafficPolicyLocal

GCE: probes [10256](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/cluster/ports/ports.go#L36)
AWS: if ELB: probes the first NodePort defined on the service spec.
Azure: probes all NodePort defined on the service spec.

All of these can be improved, but an enhancement proposal would be needed to align them all. For now: this PR will help fix some cases.

### What did you expect to happen?

Node readiness changes should not re-configure load balancers associated with services of type ETP=local. 

- Nodes not hosting any endpoints associated with these services do not forward traffic to nodes that do, so re-configuring the LB because said node goes NotReady is useless. 
- Nodes hosting endpoints associated with these services are already health checked using the HC probe configured for the `healthCheckNodePort` and can rely on that much more dynamically without needing to re-configure the LB. 

In the long-term: all load balancers should not be re-configured because of node state changes. That will need an enhancement proposal however (which I am currently drafting) to change service proxies and align cloud provider HCs. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

"as minimally and precisely as possible" not sure if this hits the definition, but: we need a big cluster with a lot of entropy (for example by performing an upgrade and restarting all nodes one-by-one) - this should end up re-configuring every single LB N*M (where N is the amount of nodes and M is the amount of state transitions per node). 

### Anything else we need to know?

### Kubernetes version

All versions.


### Cloud provider

All cloud providers. 

### OS version

<details>

```console
# On Linux:
$ cat /etc/os-release
# paste output here
$ uname -a
# paste output here

# On Windows:
C:\> wmic os get Caption, Version, BuildNumber, OSArchitecture
# paste output here
```

</details>

I am doubtful I should open a new issue for this (seeing as how it's very much correlated to this issue), but there's another problem exherbitated by re-configuring the LB when not really needed; 

Updating a service from `ExternalTrafficPolicy = Cluster` to `ExternalTrafficPolicy = Local` can/will cause minute-wide blackouts for the service SLAs.

Specifically, when such an update is issued on the service object: kube-proxy will update all rules on nodes not hosting any endpoint and stop traffic from being forwarded, this is "the fast path". Inefficiently however, the CCM will also trigger a re-configuration of the LBs HC, which is the "slow path". Any client attempting to connect to the application backed by this service will not be able to until the LB is fully re-configured, since the LB won't have an HC or an incomplete one not being able to fully indicate where traffic should be sent. It feels ridiculous that such a small change can lead to such high windows of observed downtime - this is particularly impactful on low latency applications with strict SLAs.  

This can't be fixed today without that enhancement proposal, but I think that in an ideal world (hopefully once the KEP is in) the HC for what concerns the LB should remain the same. The only real change should, on such an update, be the service proxy's response to that HC. That would severely reduce the observed "downtime". That obviously means impacting the `healthCheckNodePort`, since that port will need to be aligned with the default HC port for ETP!=Local services. At the same time users can specify what that port should be, so maybe the default port should change if the service has a `healthCheckNodePort` already defined? Te be discussed on the KEP...
